title: Estrada: Why was I convicted?
primary_topics: Erap-encounter biographical column July 7, 2013 -- second of two-part Estrada arc (A454 June 30 → A453 July 7), now in personal-anecdote register

Estrada-as-phenomenon framing: school dropout (no college diploma to prop him up), celebrated actor, charismatic politician -- town mayor (1967-1986) + senator (1987-1992) + VP (1992-1998) + president (1998-2001) + Manila mayor (2013-2016)

Ousted-and-convicted summary: abbreviated presidency by aborted Senate impeachment → Edsa II People Power Revolution → 'controversial fall' Jan 20, 2001 → SC 13-0 March 2, 2001 upheld ouster (Why? deserves another full column); plunder conviction Sept 12, 2007 → GMA pardon Oct 25, 2007 → walked free Oct 26
2010 second-place to PNoy (bested Manuel Villar + 6 others); 2013 Manila mayor victory May 13

First formal meeting Dec 3, 2007 (two months post-detention, year after CJP retirement) at Hotel InterContinental Manila 75th birthday party of former Rep. Albertito Lopez (valued client when CJP still practicing pre-SC)

Affable-encounter narrative: CJP felt 'rather awkward... as retired chief justice I had personified the judiciary that sentenced him to reclusion perpetua'; Erap cordial/polite/deferential; broke ice asking about CJ Narvasa post-Jany's death

Erap's Tagalog quip on Narvasa's depression vs his own ex-convict-but-not-lonely status: 'Yan ang mahirap sa iisa ang minamahal at iisa ang nagmamahal. Di tulad ko, marami ang minamahal at marami rin ang nagmamahal, kaya hindi ako nalulungkot kahit ex-convict' -- CJP apologized to Dr Loi who retorted 'Walang problema, sanay na ako diyan'

Most memorable Erap question: 'Chief Justice, why was I convicted of plunder and sentenced to a life in jail when I was charged merely with receiving (1) broker's commissions in sale of listed shares owned by Social Security System, and (2) jueteng money? Assuming this is true, how can I be guilty of any crime when I did not steal public funds? Wala po akong ninakaw na pera ng bayan'; CJP referred him to 262-page Sandiganbayan decision + 'by accepting pardon, deemed to have accepted judgment and imposed penalty'

People's-verdict populist-defense: trial took 6+ years in detention; pardon-acceptance freed him 'to seek the people's verdict by running again for public office'; 'In his populist mind, all government officials are ultimately judged by the people, not by the courts'; family-electoral-vindication evidence -- Loi/Jinggoy as senators, JV (son by Guia Gomez) as congressman/senator

CJP's caveat: 'Estrada cannot completely ignore the judgments of our courts and of history'; had he won 2010 presidency, SC would have decided disqualification (instead of mootness-dismissal); now mayor, 'he can no longer avoid scrutiny of the Supreme Court'; 'rule of law and democracy are intertwined and inseparable'; 'I do not necessarily agree with his unorthodox views but I respect his folksy way of articulating them. Freedom is not only for the ideas we adore but also for those we may abhor'; 76-year-old 'last hurrah' Manila mayor will vindicate him 'from villain to hero' in eyes of masa and intelligencia

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the second installment of his two-part Estrada arc -- a personal-anecdote follow-up to last week's A454 doctrinal column on the Estrada-Comelec-Jalosjos enigma, now revealing his unprecedented December 2007 first encounter with the ex-president and the conversations that followed. Joseph Ejercito Estrada is a phenomenon. A school dropout (with no college diploma to prop him up), celebrated actor and charismatic politician, he was elected and served as town mayor (1967-1986), senator (1987-1992), vice president (1992-1998), president (1998-2001), and now mayor of Manila (2013-2016). Ousted and convicted: though elected overwhelmingly, his presidency was abbreviated by an aborted Senate impeachment trial, which led to the Edsa II People Power Revolution and, eventually, to his controversial fall on Jan 20, 2001; on March 2, 2001, the SC, voting 13-0, upheld his ouster from the top post (why? well, that question deserves another full column). Thereafter, he was charged with and convicted of plunder on Sept 12, 2007, but was pardoned on Oct 25, 2007 by President GMA; the next day, Oct 26, he walked free. He ran for president in 2010, placed second to Benigno Aquino III, but bested early favorite Manuel Villar and six others; undaunted by his only defeat in his long political career, he ran and won as Manila's mayor last May 13. CJ had a nodding, so-so acquaintance with him since he was a senator, but formally met and conversed with him only on Dec 3, 2007, two months after he was released from detention and a year after CJ retired from the judiciary -- this was during the 75th birthday party at Hotel InterContinental Manila of former Rep. Albertito Lopez, a valued client when CJ was still practicing law prior to his SC stint. Affable encounter: CJ felt rather awkward encountering him at that point when he was just released from detention -- as a retired Chief Justice, CJ had personified the judiciary that sentenced him to reclusion perpetua; but Erap did not seem to mind the surprise encounter -- in fact, he was cordial, polite and deferential. Seated opposite CJ across the rectangular head table, he broke the ice by asking how retired CJ Andres R. Narvasa was; CJ replied that after his wife Jany passed away, Narvasa had been inaccessible and depressed -- to which Erap quipped, 'Yan ang mahirap sa iisa ang minamahal at iisa ang nagmamahal. Di tulad ko, marami ang minamahal at marami rin ang nagmamahal, kaya hindi ako nalulungkot kahit ex-convict.' Embarrassed at the quip made in the presence of his wife seated beside him, CJ apologized, 'Pasensiya na po kayo, Doctora Loi, nagbibiro lang po si Presidente'; to which she gamely retorted, 'Walang problema, sanay na ako diyan' -- that exchange set an affable tone for the rest of the evening. At his request, they met a few times thereafter; he posited pointed questions from which CJ got an insight into his mindset and why he exemplifies and speaks for the masa. One of the most memorable questions he asked was, 'Chief Justice, why was I convicted of plunder and sentenced to a life in jail when I was charged merely with receiving (1) the broker's commissions in the sale of listed shares owned by the Social Security System, and (2) jueteng money? Assuming this is true, how can I be guilty of any crime when I did not steal public funds? Wala po akong ninakaw na pera ng bayan.' CJ replied that the 262-page decision of the Sandiganbayan completely answered his question -- it eloquently spoke for itself; CJ could not add or subtract anything more; in any event, if he disagreed with the verdict, he should have appealed to the SC; by accepting the pardon, he was deemed to have also accepted the judgment and the imposed penalty. People's verdict: Erap explained in his best Tagalog that his trial took more than six years while he was in detention -- had he appealed, he would have had to suffer many more years of detention without any assurance of victory; on the other hand, by accepting the pardon, he became free to seek the people's verdict by running again for public office; he preferred a direct redemption by the people. In his populist mind, all government officials are ultimately judged by the people, not by the courts -- once elected to public office, he would have been exonerated by the people, the real sovereigns of our democracy; this explains his eagerness to run for president in 2010 and for mayor in 2013; even already, the poll victory of his wife Loi and son Jinggoy as senators, and of JV (his son by Guia Gomez) as congressman and later also as senator, are proofs of his popular vindication. Be that as it may, CJ thinks Estrada cannot completely ignore the judgments of our courts and of history -- had he won the presidency in 2010, the SC would have decided his disqualification case, instead of dismissing it for having become moot after his defeat; but now, with his victory as mayor, he can no longer avoid the scrutiny of the SC (see CJ's column last Sunday, A454); indeed, the rule of law and democracy are intertwined and inseparable. They discussed many other interesting topics, which provided CJ a window to see why, despite his ouster from the presidency, his plunder conviction, and his open marital peccadilloes, he continues to be the darling of the masang Pilipino -- CJ does not necessarily agree with his unorthodox views but respects his folksy way of articulating them; 'freedom is not only for the ideas we adore but also for those we may abhor.' At 76, he thinks his 'last hurrah' as Manila mayor will vindicate him in history and will presage his passage from villain to hero in the eyes of both the masa and the intelligencia -- this, CJ will await and see.
